newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile to discuss Latam rules for Pacific fishing.
newsitem.headline: Chile to discuss Latam rules for Pacific fishing.

text.p: Chile has started discussing new rules on fishing in the Pacific Ocean with countries along Latin America's west coast following Santiago's decision to reject a U.N. pact on high seas catches, a top official said Friday.
"The result of the U.N. agreement was not what Chile was hoping for," Fishing Undersecretary Juan Manuel Cruz told a news conference.
"We are studying our options. We have started the process of consultation with the countries of the South Pacific group."
Chile is a member of the Permanent Commission on the South Pacific which also groups Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.
The Pacific waters off the region's west coast are among the world's richest fishing grounds.

Chilean Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza said Thursday that Chile had decided not to sign the United Nations Convention on Transzonal and Highly Migratory Fish, known as the New York accord, as it would not give enough protection to the country's fish stocks.
The agreement seeks to regulate catching migratory species outside a country's 200 mile exclusive fishing zone.
Chile fears that the rules will allow foreign fleets to catch fish like mackerel which migrate regularly from the high seas towards its northern coasts.
"We want measures which allow the conservation and avoid the depletion of species which migrate into and outside the exclusive economic zone," said Insulza in newspaper Estrategia.
Insulza said Chile would propose that the countries from the commission strike their own deal to preserve the region's fishing grounds.

Chile's own fish stocks have been heavily depleted by overfishing in the 1980s and early 1990s. The government now controls fishing seasons and imposes temporary bans if fishing poses a threat to stocks.
Chile is the world's second largest fishmeal producer with its fleets catching over six million tonnes of fish last year.
